$$
∇f(x,y)=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\,i+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\,j.
$$

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y+\operatorname{sin}⁡y
$$

First, we integrate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ with respect to $x.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & =\int \frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y+g(y)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to $y,$ we obtain

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y+{g}^{′}(y).
$$

Taking  $$
\displaystyle \frac{∂f}{∂y}=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y+\operatorname{sin}⁡y

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y+{g}^{′}(y) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y+\operatorname{sin}⁡y \\ {g}^{′}(y) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡y \\ g(y) & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡y+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

Finally, substituting $g(y)=-\operatorname{cos}⁡y+C$ into our expression for $f(x,y),$ we get

$$
f(x,y)=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y-\operatorname{cos}⁡y+C.

\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x{z}^{2}+\frac{∂g}{∂y}

$$
\begin{aligned}x{z}^{2}+\frac{∂g}{∂y} & =x{z}^{2}+z \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =z\end{aligned}

question.:question/problem:
Find the general form of $f(x,y)$ on $\mathbb R^2$ such that

$$
\nabla f=(2xy)\,\mathbf i+(x^2-2y)\,\mathbf j.
$$

Integrating the first component with respect to $x$ gives $f(x,y)=x^2y+g(y)$. Use the second component to determine $g(y)$ and select $f(x,y)$. In the choices, $C$ is an arbitrary constant.
question.:question/worked-solution:
The components of $\nabla f$ are $f_x$ and $f_y$. Integrating $f_x$ with respect to $x$, treating $y$ as constant, leaves an arbitrary function $g(y)$ because its $x$-derivative is zero.

Here $f_x=2xy$ and $f_y=x^2-2y$, so

$$
f(x,y)=\int 2xy\,\mathrm dx=x^2y+g(y).
$$

Differentiate with respect to $y$ and match the second component:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x^2+g'(y)&=x^2-2y\\
g'(y)&=-2y\\
g(y)&=-y^2+C.
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus

$$
f(x,y)=x^2y-y^2+C.
$$

Checking both components gives $f_x=2xy$ and $f_y=x^2-2y$, as required.

question.:question/problem:
Find the general form of $f(x,y)$ on $\mathbb R^2$ such that

$$
\nabla f=(2xy+y^2+1)\,\mathbf i+(x^2+2xy+3y^2)\,\mathbf j.
$$

In the choices, $C$ is an arbitrary constant.
question.:question/worked-solution:
The components of $\nabla f$ are $f_x$ and $f_y$. Integrating $f_x$ with respect to $x$, treating $y$ as constant, leaves an arbitrary function $g(y)$ because its $x$-derivative is zero.

The two required partial derivatives are $f_x=2xy+y^2+1$ and $f_y=x^2+2xy+3y^2$. Integrate the first:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f(x,y)&=\int(2xy+y^2+1)\,\mathrm dx\\
&=x^2y+xy^2+x+g(y).
\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating this expression with respect to $y$ and using the second component gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
x^2+2xy+g'(y)&=x^2+2xy+3y^2\\
g'(y)&=3y^2\\
g(y)&=y^3+C.
\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute to obtain

$$
f(x,y)=x^2y+xy^2+x+y^3+C.
$$

Verification gives

$$
f_x=2xy+y^2+1,\qquad f_y=x^2+2xy+3y^2.
$$

Omitting $y^3$ would preserve $f_x$ but fail to supply $3y^2$ in $f_y$. Omitting $x$ would preserve $f_y$ but lose the constant $1$ in $f_x$. Both components matter.

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z)&=\int \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\,\mathrm{d}x \\ &=\int \left(- 2 y\right)\,\mathrm{d}x \\ &=- 2 x y+g(y,z)\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}=- 2 x+\frac{\partial g}{\partial y}.
